claim: The pleasure of a reward in humans is hypothesized to be mediated by an opioidergic system involving the hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens and the amygdala
source: It has been hypothesized that the pleasure of a reward in humans is mediated by an opioidergic system involving the hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens and the amygdala.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the abstract, drawing on existing theoretical frameworks

claim: Enjoying the pleasure of a reward is distinct from incentive salience induced by cues predicting the reward
source: Importantly, enjoying the pleasure of a reward is distinct from incentive salience induced by cues predicting the reward.
evidence: This distinction is stated as an established concept in the abstract

claim: Blocking opioid receptors reduced pleasure associated with viewing erotic pictures more than viewing symbols of reward such as money
source: Our data show that blocking opioid receptors reduced pleasure associated with viewing erotic pictures more than viewing symbols of reward such as money.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data

claim: Naloxone-induced reduction in pleasure was paralleled by a reduction of activation in the ventral striatum, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, amygdala, hypothalamus and medial prefrontal cortex
source: This was paralleled by a reduction of activation in the ventral striatum, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, amygdala, hypothalamus and medial prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from fMRI data reported in the abstract

claim: The naloxone induced activation decrease was observed at reward delivery, but not during reward anticipation
source: Crucially, the naloxone induced activation decrease was observed at reward delivery, but not during reward anticipation, indicating that blocking opioid receptors decreases the pleasure of rewards in humans.
evidence: This temporal specificity is a key finding from the experimental data

claim: Blocking opioid receptors decreases the pleasure of rewards in humans
source: Crucially, the naloxone induced activation decrease was observed at reward delivery, but not during reward anticipation, indicating that blocking opioid receptors decreases the pleasure of rewards in humans.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings

claim: Goal directed behaviors such as finding a sexual mate or searching for food are crucial for survival and subserved by a mainly dopaminergic motivational system including the ventral striatum
source: Goal directed behaviors such as finding a sexual mate or searching for food are crucial for survival and subserved by a mainly dopaminergic motivational system including the ventral striatum (Morton et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morton et al., 2006

claim: In rodents, the pleasure of goal directed behaviors (the hedonic aspect of reward consumption) is mediated by an additional, opioidergic system
source: However, in the rodent it has been shown that the ensuing pleasure of these goal directed behaviors that is the hedonic aspect of reward consumption is mediated by an additional, opioidergic system (Peciña and Berridge, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peciña and Berridge, 2005

claim: Opioids play an important role in reproduction, an effect mainly mediated by the hypothalamus and amygdala
source: This is in line with the observation that opioids play an important role in reproduction, an effect mainly mediated by the hypothalamus and amygdala (Kostarczyk, 1986; Le Merrer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kostarczyk, 1986 and Le Merrer et al., 2009

claim: Behavioral studies employing opioid antagonists suggest a role of endogenous opioids in relationship to positively valenced stimuli such as attractive faces
source: In humans, behavioral studies employing opioid antagonists suggest a role of endogenous opioids in relationship to positively valenced stimuli such as attractive faces (Chelnokova et al., 2014), food (Yeomans and Gray, 2002) and social aspects (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chelnokova et al., 2014

claim: Behavioral studies employing opioid antagonists suggest a role of endogenous opioids in relationship to food
source: In humans, behavioral studies employing opioid antagonists suggest a role of endogenous opioids in relationship to positively valenced stimuli such as attractive faces (Chelnokova et al., 2014), food (Yeomans and Gray, 2002) and social aspects (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yeomans and Gray, 2002

claim: Behavioral studies employing opioid antagonists suggest a role of endogenous opioids in relationship to social aspects
source: In humans, behavioral studies employing opioid antagonists suggest a role of endogenous opioids in relationship to positively valenced stimuli such as attractive faces (Chelnokova et al., 2014), food (Yeomans and Gray, 2002) and social aspects (Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hsu et al., 2013

claim: Evidence with respect to the role of opioids in reward processing in humans is contradictory
source: However, evidence with respect to the role of opioids in reward processing in humans is contradictory, as some studies show negative effects of opioid blockade on reward processing (Petrovic et al., 2008), whereas others have shown positive effects (Porchet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing conflicting results

claim: Some studies show negative effects of opioid blockade on reward processing
source: However, evidence with respect to the role of opioids in reward processing in humans is contradictory, as some studies show negative effects of opioid blockade on reward processing (Petrovic et al., 2008), whereas others have shown positive effects (Porchet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petrovic et al., 2008

claim: Some studies have shown positive effects of opioid blockade on reward processing
source: However, evidence with respect to the role of opioids in reward processing in humans is contradictory, as some studies show negative effects of opioid blockade on reward processing (Petrovic et al., 2008), whereas others have shown positive effects (Porchet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Porchet et al., 2013

claim: Human neuroimaging studies using PET with an opioid tracer have revealed a correlation between social acceptance and activity in the ventral striatum and the amygdala
source: Additionally, human neuroimaging studies using positron emission tomography with an opioid tracer have revealed a correlation between social acceptance (Hsu et al., 2013), positive emotions induced by erotic stimuli (Koepp et al., 2009) or food (Nummenmaa et al., 2018) and activity in the ventral striatum and the amygdala.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hsu et al., 2013

claim: Human neuroimaging studies using PET with an opioid tracer have revealed a correlation between positive emotions induced by erotic stimuli and activity in the ventral striatum and the amygdala
source: Additionally, human neuroimaging studies using positron emission tomography with an opioid tracer have revealed a correlation between social acceptance (Hsu et al., 2013), positive emotions induced by erotic stimuli (Koepp et al., 2009) or food (Nummenmaa et al., 2018) and activity in the ventral striatum and the amygdala.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koepp et al., 2009

claim: Human neuroimaging studies using PET with an opioid tracer have revealed a correlation between food and activity in the ventral striatum and the amygdala
source: Additionally, human neuroimaging studies using positron emission tomography with an opioid tracer have revealed a correlation between social acceptance (Hsu et al., 2013), positive emotions induced by erotic stimuli (Koepp et al., 2009) or food (Nummenmaa et al., 2018) and activity in the ventral striatum and the amygdala.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nummenmaa et al., 2018

claim: PET studies have not been able to dissociate the temporal aspects of reward processing such as the effects during anticipation reflecting incentive salience and the hedonic aspects or pleasure related to a reward
source: However, PET studies have not been able to dissociate the temporal aspects of reward processing such as the effects during anticipation reflecting incentive salience and the hedonic aspects or pleasure related to a reward.
evidence: This is a limitation of PET methodology stated based on knowledge of the technique

claim: Previous animal studies have revealed a temporally distinct response pattern of the mesolimbic system in particular dissociating responses for reward anticipation and outcome
source: This dissociation is neurobiologically important, as previous animal studies have revealed a temporally distinct response pattern of the mesolimbic system in particular dissociating responses for reward anticipation and outcome (Schultz et al., 1997; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schultz et al., 1997 and Smith et al., 2011

claim: Anticipatory or conditioned stimuli that predict a reward are associated with incentive salience
source: In this context, it has been shown that anticipatory or conditioned stimuli that predict a reward are associated with incentive salience, but only the actual reward delivery (sucrose) was associated with hedonic effects (Peciña and Berridge, 2005; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peciña and Berridge, 2005 and Smith et al., 2011

claim: Only the actual reward delivery (sucrose) was associated with hedonic effects
source: In this context, it has been shown that anticipatory or conditioned stimuli that predict a reward are associated with incentive salience, but only the actual reward delivery (sucrose) was associated with hedonic effects (Peciña and Berridge, 2005; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peciña and Berridge, 2005 and Smith et al., 2011

claim: The hedonic effect linked to the outcome phase was exclusively opioid dependent
source: More importantly, the hedonic effect linked to the outcome phase was exclusively opioid dependent, whereas the effect of incentive salience during anticipation was also dopamine dependent.
evidence: This is stated as an important finding from previous research

claim: The effect of incentive salience during anticipation was also dopamine dependent
source: More importantly, the hedonic effect linked to the outcome phase was exclusively opioid dependent, whereas the effect of incentive salience during anticipation was also dopamine dependent.
evidence: This is stated as an important finding from previous research

claim: In humans, anticipation and outcome related neuronal effects can reliably be dissociated by fMRI
source: In humans, anticipation and outcome related neuronal effects can reliably be dissociated by fMRI (Knutson et al., 2000; Yacubian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knutson et al., 2000 and Yacubian et al., 2006

claim: Erotic stimuli directly resemble a pleasurable reward
source: To even further dissociate incentive salience from reward related pleasure, we compared erotic stimuli, which directly resemble a pleasurable reward to pictures of monetary outcomes, which are merely visual representations of what a participant can redeem after the experiment (Sescousse et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental design, supported by citation

claim: Pictures of monetary outcomes are merely visual representations of what a participant can redeem after the experiment
source: To even further dissociate incentive salience from reward related pleasure, we compared erotic stimuli, which directly resemble a pleasurable reward to pictures of monetary outcomes, which are merely visual representations of what a participant can redeem after the experiment (Sescousse et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental design, supported by citation

claim: Erotic pictures have been shown to reliably activate the mesolimbic system
source: Consequently, we extended the well-established monetary incentive delay task (Knutson et al., 2000) with erotic pictures, which have been shown to reliably activate the mesolimbic system (Redouté et al., 2000; Beauregard et al., 2001; Arnow et al., 2002; Hamann et al., 2004; Ponseti et al., 2006; Paul et al., 2008; Sescousse et al., 2010; Sescousse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations

claim: Twenty-one heterosexual, healthy, male volunteers (mean age 25.5 years) took part in the experiment
source: Twenty-one heterosexual, healthy, male volunteers (mean age 25.5 years) took part in the experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample

claim: Behavioral mood and side effects ratings did not differ between treatments
source: Behavioral mood and side effects ratings did not differ between treatments (Supplementary file 1 & 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis

claim: Volunteers perceived high erotic stimuli (total nudity) as more pleasurable compared to low erotic (swimsuit) stimuli in the placebo condition
source: Hedonic ratings in the placebo condition indicated that volunteers perceived high erotic stimuli (total nudity) as more pleasurable compared to low erotic (swimsuit) stimuli (mean high erotic >low erotic: T(18)=7.74; p<0.00001).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data with statistical support

claim: Skin conductance data showed significantly higher values for erotic rewards as compared to monetary rewards
source: Interestingly, skin conductance data showed the opposite pattern, with significantly higher values for erotic rewards as compared to monetary rewards (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from autonomic data analysis, referenced to Figure 2

claim: A high erotic reward induced a significantly stronger SCR response as compared to a high monetary reward
source: In particular, a high erotic reward induced a significantly stronger SCR response as compared to a high monetary reward (T(13)= 2.87; p=0.007; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from autonomic data with statistical support

claim: Low erotic rewards induced significantly stronger SCR responses compared to low monetary rewards
source: The same was observed comparing low erotic to low monetary rewards (T(13)= 3.16; p=0.004).
evidence: This is a finding from autonomic data with statistical support

claim: Only weak SCR responses were observed for the anticipation phase
source: In addition, only weak responses were observed for the anticipation phase (i.e. evoked by the cue).
evidence: This is a finding from autonomic data analysis

claim: Volunteers' ratings on sensitive items such as erotic pictures have been shown to be influenced by social desirability
source: This discrepancy was not unexpected as volunteers' ratings on sensitive items such as erotic pictures have been shown to be influenced by social desirability (Tourangeau and Yan, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tourangeau and Yan, 2007

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA revealed a main effect of condition on pleasure ratings
source: A repeated measures ANOVA with factors treatment and condition (Supplementary file 4) revealed a main effect of condition F(3.94, 67.12) = 16.709; p=1.79*10−09, a trend for a main effect of treatment F(1,17)=4.06; p=0.06 and importantly a treatment by condition interaction F(5.22, 88.68)=2.60; p=0.03.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA revealed a trend for a main effect of treatment on pleasure ratings
source: A repeated measures ANOVA with factors treatment and condition (Supplementary file 4) revealed a main effect of condition F(3.94, 67.12) = 16.709; p=1.79*10−09, a trend for a main effect of treatment F(1,17)=4.06; p=0.06 and importantly a treatment by condition interaction F(5.22, 88.68)=2.60; p=0.03.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA revealed a treatment by condition interaction on pleasure ratings
source: A repeated measures ANOVA with factors treatment and condition (Supplementary file 4) revealed a main effect of condition F(3.94, 67.12) = 16.709; p=1.79*10−09, a trend for a main effect of treatment F(1,17)=4.06; p=0.06 and importantly a treatment by condition interaction F(5.22, 88.68)=2.60; p=0.03.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis

claim: Pleasure ratings at the outcome phase in gain trials were reduced during naloxone treatment
source: In particular, pleasure ratings at the outcome phase of the experiment, that is directly after viewing the erotic picture, in gain trials were reduced during naloxone treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis

claim: The effect of naloxone on pleasure ratings was most pronounced for the high pleasure condition
source: This effect was most pronounced for the high pleasure condition (T(18)=3.90; p<0.001; Figure 3; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data with statistical support

claim: Motivation to attain a goal has been shown to affect the level of frustration when thwarted
source: Motivation to attain a goal has been shown to affect the level of frustration when thwarted (Dollard et al., 1939).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dollard et al., 1939

claim: Naloxone significantly reduced frustration ratings when erotic pictures were not shown in missed reward trials
source: We therefore also investigated whether naloxone has an effect on frustration ratings, that is when in missed reward trials the erotic picture was not shown, and observed a significant reduction by naloxone (T(18)=2.80; p<0.006).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data with statistical support

claim: Naloxone caused a significantly stronger reduction of frustration ratings for missed erotic rewards compared to missed monetary rewards
source: In addition we observed a significantly stronger reduction of frustration ratings for the missed reward trials for erotic as compared to monetary outcomes (T(18)=2.61; p=0.0088; Figure 3 right; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data with statistical support

claim: Naloxone reduced BOLD responses to erotic image presentation in bilateral ventral striatum at the outcome phase
source: Our analysis revealed a reduction of BOLD responses by naloxone to erotic image presentation in bilateral ventral striatum at the outcome phase (right: T(18)=2.99; p=0.004; p(corrected)=0.031; left: T(18)=3.47; p=0.001; p(corrected)=0.011; Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data with statistical support

claim: Naloxone reduced BOLD responses to erotic image presentation in lateral OFC at the outcome phase
source: Our analysis revealed a reduction of BOLD responses by naloxone to erotic image presentation in bilateral ventral striatum at the outcome phase (right: T(18)=2.99; p=0.004; p(corrected)=0.031; left: T(18)=3.47; p=0.001; p(corrected)=0.011; Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), lateral OFC (right: T(18)=2.84; p=0.006; p(corrected)=0.044; left: T(18)=1.94; p=0.034; p(corrected)=0.275)
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data with statistical support

claim: Naloxone reduced BOLD responses to erotic image presentation in bilateral amygdalae at the outcome phase
source: Our analysis revealed a reduction of BOLD responses by naloxone to erotic image presentation in bilateral ventral striatum at the outcome phase (right: T(18)=2.99; p=0.004; p(corrected)=0.031; left: T(18)=3.47; p=0.001; p(corrected)=0.011; Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), lateral OFC (right: T(18)=2.84; p=0.006; p(corrected)=0.044; left: T(18)=1.94; p=0.034; p(corrected)=0.275), bilateral amygdalae (right: T(18)=2.85; p=0.005; p(corrected)=0.043; left: T(18)=2.83; p=0.006; p(corrected)=0.044)
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data with statistical support

claim: Naloxone reduced BOLD responses to erotic image presentation in medial prefrontal cortex at the outcome phase
source: Our analysis revealed a reduction of BOLD responses by naloxone to erotic image presentation in bilateral ventral striatum at the outcome phase (right: T(18)=2.99; p=0.004; p(corrected)=0.031; left: T(18)=3.47; p=0.001; p(corrected)=0.011; Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), lateral OFC (right: T(18)=2.84; p=0.006; p(corrected)=0.044; left: T(18)=1.94; p=0.034; p(corrected)=0.275), bilateral amygdalae (right: T(18)=2.85; p=0.005; p(corrected)=0.043; left: T(18)=2.83; p=0.006; p(corrected)=0.044), medial prefrontal cortex (T(18)=3.52; p=0.001; p(corrected)=0.010)
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data with statistical support

claim: Naloxone reduced BOLD responses to erotic image presentation in the hypothalamus at the outcome phase
source: Our analysis revealed a reduction of BOLD responses by naloxone to erotic image presentation in bilateral ventral striatum at the outcome phase (right: T(18)=2.99; p=0.004; p(corrected)=0.031; left: T(18)=3.47; p=0.001; p(corrected)=0.011; Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), lateral OFC (right: T(18)=2.84; p=0.006; p(corrected)=0.044; left: T(18)=1.94; p=0.034; p(corrected)=0.275), bilateral amygdalae (right: T(18)=2.85; p=0.005; p(corrected)=0.043; left: T(18)=2.83; p=0.006; p(corrected)=0.044), medial prefrontal cortex (T(18)=3.52; p=0.001; p(corrected)=0.010) and the hypothalamus (T(18)=1.87; p=0.039; p(corrected)=0.309).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data with statistical support

claim: No significant effects of naloxone were observed for monetary trials at the outcome phase
source: For the monetary trials no significant effects of naloxone were observed at the outcome phase (Supplementary file 9 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis

claim: Naloxone effects on erotic rewards were stronger than its effects on monetary rewards in all regions of interest
source: Directly comparing naloxone effects on erotic rewards with its effects on monetary rewards, we observed a stronger effect of naloxone with respect to erotic rewards in all regions of interest (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 8), with the most significant effect in the amygdala (right: T(18)=3.40; p=0.0016; p(corrected)=0.0128; left: T(18)=3.50; p=0.0013; p(corrected)=0.0103).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data with statistical support

claim: The most significant differential effect of naloxone between erotic and monetary rewards was in the amygdala
source: Directly comparing naloxone effects on erotic rewards with its effects on monetary rewards, we observed a stronger effect of naloxone with respect to erotic rewards in all regions of interest (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 8), with the most significant effect in the amygdala (right: T(18)=3.40; p=0.0016; p(corrected)=0.0128; left: T(18)=3.50; p=0.0013; p(corrected)=0.0103).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data with statistical support

claim: The individual decrease of pleasure ratings due to naloxone was significantly correlated with the reduction of brain activation in the hypothalamus
source: Using a linear regression analysis (Supplementary file 10), we observed a significant correlation in the hypothalamus (T(17)=3.24; p=0.0024; p(corrected)=0.0194; Figure 5; Supplementary file 10)
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis with statistical support

claim: The individual decrease of pleasure ratings due to naloxone showed a weaker correlation with the reduction of brain activation in the left ventral striatum
source: Using a linear regression analysis (Supplementary file 10), we observed a significant correlation in the hypothalamus (T(17)=3.24; p=0.0024; p(corrected)=0.0194; Figure 5; Supplementary file 10) and a weaker correlation in the left ventral striatum (T(17)=2.09; p=0.0262; p(corrected)=0.2097; Figure 5; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis with statistical support

claim: The BOLD signal difference in the hypothalamus due to naloxone is linearly related to the individual decrease in pleasure ratings
source: This indicates that the BOLD signal difference in the hypothalamus due to naloxone is linearly related to the individual decrease in pleasure ratings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation finding

claim: Naloxone can reduce pleasure ratings in a cross-over pharmacological challenge design, causally implicating the opioidergic system in hedonic processing of erotic stimuli
source: Observing that naloxone can reduce pleasure ratings in a cross-over pharmacological challenge design causally implicates the opioidergic system in hedonic processing of erotic stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings

claim: A similar system mediates pleasure in humans as it does in rodents
source: Our findings show that a similar system mediates pleasure as it does in rodents (Peciña and Berridge, 2005; Ismail et al., 2009; Le Merrer et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings, supported by citations to rodent studies

claim: The effect of opioid antagonists on pleasurable erotic stimuli was specifically related to the outcome phase
source: Not only did we observe a strong effect of opioid antagonists on pleasurable erotic stimuli, but this effect was specifically related to the outcome phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal specificity of the findings

claim: Previous molecular imaging (PET) studies have indicated a relationship between social rejection and the opioid system
source: Elegant previous molecular imaging (PET) studies have indicated a relationship between social rejection (Hsu et al., 2013), food stimuli (Nummenmaa et al., 2018) or erotic stimulus material (Koepp et al., 2009) and the opioid system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hsu et al., 2013

claim: Previous molecular imaging (PET) studies have indicated a relationship between food stimuli and the opioid system
source: Elegant previous molecular imaging (PET) studies have indicated a relationship between social rejection (Hsu et al., 2013), food stimuli (Nummenmaa et al., 2018) or erotic stimulus material (Koepp et al., 2009) and the opioid system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nummenmaa et al., 2018

claim: Previous molecular imaging (PET) studies have indicated a relationship between erotic stimulus material and the opioid system
source: Elegant previous molecular imaging (PET) studies have indicated a relationship between social rejection (Hsu et al., 2013), food stimuli (Nummenmaa et al., 2018) or erotic stimulus material (Koepp et al., 2009) and the opioid system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koepp et al., 2009

claim: PET studies were not in a position to answer whether reward anticipation or outcome is responsible for opioid effects due to the nature of the imaging modality
source: However, by the nature of the imaging modality, these studies were not in a position to answer the crucial question of whether reward anticipation or outcome is responsible for the observed effect.
evidence: This is a limitation of PET methodology stated based on knowledge

claim: The high temporal resolution of pharmacological fMRI allowed dissociation of the anticipation from the outcome phase
source: The rather high temporal resolution of our pharmacological fMRI approach allowed us to dissociate the anticipation from the outcome phase and thus to attribute hedonic reward processing to an opioidergic system.
evidence: This is a methodological advantage of the current study

claim: In a sequential conditioning task in rodents, hedonic effects were only observed for the outcome phase, but neither for CS1 nor CS2
source: In a sequential conditioning task in rodents in which a first conditioned stimulus (CS1) was followed by a second (CS2) which was then followed by a sucrose reward, it could be demonstrated that hedonic effects were only observed for the outcome phase, but neither for CS1 nor CS2 (Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2011

claim: Incentive salience attribution was higher for cues more proximal to the actual reward in rodent studies
source: This study has also shown that incentive salience attribution was higher for cues more proximal to the actual reward (i.e. CS2) and although responses to the CS increased after opioid stimulation of the Nacc, they remained much smaller as compared to sucrose reward.
evidence: This is a finding from rodent studies cited in the discussion

claim: The effect of incentive salience at CS2 was dopamine and opioid dependent in rodent studies
source: Furthermore, the effect of incentive salience at CS2 was dopamine and opioid dependent, whereas the hedonic effect linked to the outcome phase was only opioid dependent.
evidence: This is a finding from rodent studies cited in the discussion

claim: An important property of erotic pictures is that they directly resemble a reward
source: It has been argued (Sescousse et al., 2010) that an important property of erotic pictures is that they directly resemble a reward, which is in contrast to pictures of monetary outcomes that are merely visual representations of what the participant can redeem after the experiment.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sescousse et al., 2010

claim: Smith and colleagues observed weak to non-existing facial responses indicative of hedonic processing for CS1 and CS2, but strong responses for the sucrose reward
source: Smith and colleagues (Smith et al., 2011) observed weak to non-existing facial responses indicative of hedonic processing for CS1 and CS2, but strong responses for the sucrose reward.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2011

claim: Pharmacological manipulation of the human opioid system can affect motivation for viewing opposite-sex faces
source: With respect to opposite sex human stimuli, a design involving attractive faces offered first evidence that pharmacological manipulation of the human opioid system can affect motivation for viewing opposite-sex faces (Chelnokova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chelnokova et al., 2014

claim: A study involving affective pictures including erotic material could not reveal an effect of naloxone on pleasure ratings
source: In contrast to these findings, a study involving affective pictures, which included erotic material, could not reveal an effect of naloxone on pleasure ratings (Kut et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kut et al., 2011

claim: The role of opioids in mediating pleasure is modulated by motivational aspects
source: This suggests that the role of opioids in mediating pleasure is modulated by motivational aspects, analogous to observations in the dopaminergic system (Coricelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing studies, supported by a citation

claim: Previous studies observed a correlation of hypothalamic activity with pleasure ratings and penile tumescence in the context of visual erotic stimuli
source: Previous studies observed a correlation of hypothalamic activity with pleasure ratings and penile tumescence in the context of visual erotic stimuli (Redouté et al., 2000; Arnow et al., 2002; Paul et al., 2008; Georgiadis et al., 2012) and direct sexual activity (Georgiadis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations

claim: The hypothalamic effect on pleasure ratings for erotic stimuli is mediated by opioids
source: Importantly, our data suggests that this effect is mediated by opioids, because the individual reduction of pleasure ratings for erotic stimuli by naloxone was correlated with the reduction of brain activation in the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation finding

claim: The hypothalamus is an important structure for behavioral, autonomic and endocrine responses in relation to reproductive behavior
source: The hypothalamus is an important structure for behavioral, autonomic and endocrine responses in relation to reproductive behavior (Le Merrer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Le Merrer et al., 2009

claim: Opioid receptor agonists injected directly into the hypothalamus inhibited or delayed sexual behavior in rodents
source: Opioid receptor agonists injected directly into the hypothalamus inhibited or delayed sexual behavior (van Furth et al., 1995; Le Merrer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Furth et al., 1995 and Le Merrer et al., 2009

claim: Opioid antagonists facilitate male sexual behavior
source: In contrast, opioid antagonists facilitate male sexual behavior.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from rodent studies

claim: Opioid receptor antagonists but not dopamine antagonists in the hypothalamus can block conditioned place preference linked to sexual behavior in rodents
source: In addition, rodent studies have revealed that opioid receptor antagonists (Agmo and Gómez, 1993) but not dopamine antagonists (Ismail et al., 2009) in the hypothalamus can block conditioned place preference (CPP) linked to sexual behavior
evidence: This is supported by citations to Agmo and Gómez, 1993 and Ismail et al., 2009

claim: There is a distributed system of hypothalamic and limbic regions for mediating the effects of sexual rewards
source: In addition, rodent studies have revealed that opioid receptor antagonists (Agmo and Gómez, 1993) but not dopamine antagonists (Ismail et al., 2009) in the hypothalamus can block conditioned place preference (CPP) linked to sexual behavior, indicating a distributed system of hypothalamic and limbic regions for mediating the effects of sexual rewards (Le Merrer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Le Merrer et al., 2009

claim: Sexual behavior in rodents is increased by opioid antagonists
source: Given that sexual behavior in rodents is increased by opioid antagonists, whereas we observed decreased pleasure in viewing of erotic pictures under naloxone emphasizes that additional processes contribute to sexual behavior as compared to viewing erotic pictures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from rodent studies

claim: Infusion of an opioid antagonist into the nucleus accumbens did not reduce the reinforcing properties of ejaculation
source: The pivotal role of the hypothalamus is further underlined by the observation that infusion of an opioid antagonist into the nucleus accumbens did not reduce the reinforcing properties of ejaculation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research

claim: The hypothalamus is the site where sexual reward is produced
source: This strong observation led the authors to conclude that the hypothalamus is the site where sexual reward is produced (Agmo and Gómez, 1993).
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous research, supported by citation

claim: Showing that an opioid antagonist can block differential responses for high versus low erotic stimuli directly implies opioids in mediating these effects
source: Therefore, showing that an opioid antagonist can block differential responses for high versus low erotic stimuli directly implies opioids in mediating these effects.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design and findings

claim: The effect of an opioid antagonist was strongest for the most valuable stimuli
source: Furthermore, our behavioral data is in line with previous studies, showing that the effect of an opioid antagonist was strongest for the most valuable stimuli (Chelnokova et al., 2014).
